title: Gathin23/cleanyourtv
author: Gathin23
body:
**The viral tweet:** [x.com/gathint/status/2111379569030939102](https://x.com/gathint/status/2111379569030939102) On 17 October 2026 I posted a before and after of my parents' TV, cleaned up by Claude Code over Wi-Fi. It reached 7.4M views, people started doing the same to their own TVs, and their replies turned into the lists here: 170+ TV models from 200+ contributors in four days. The repo was called tv-vibehack until the 19th; old links work. ## How it works Android TVs have the same debug bridge as Android phones. Switch on USB debugging in the TV's developer options, allow your computer once, and the rest is standard Android tooling: | Step | What happens | |---|---| | **Back up** | The list of installed packages and settings. | | **Disable** | The manufacturer's telemetry, ad services, content rows and preloaded junk, with `pm disable-user`. Nothing is uninstalled, so a restore script can undo every step. | | **Install** | A small native launcher, made the default home screen. | **No root, no cable, nothing uninstalled, and a one-line restore if you change your mind.** The bloat differs by brand, so the prompt has your coding assistant discover it on your TV and ask before touching anything you might use. ## Quick start You need a computer on the same Wi-Fi as the TV and a coding assistant with shell access. Any of these work: Claude Code (on [0G Private Computer](https://pc.0g.ai) or an [Anthropic plan](https://claude.com/pricing)), [Codex](https://github.com/openai/codex) or [Gemini CLI](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli). | Where | What to do | |---|---| | **1. On the TV** | Settings → Device Preferences → About → press OK on **Build** seven times → back → Developer options → **USB debugging** on. If you see a Network or ADB debugging toggle, turn that on too. Keep the TV on. | | **2. On your computer** | Paste [`PROMPT.md`](PROMPT.md) into your assistant and fill in your TV model. | | **3. Follow along** | Accept "Allow USB debugging?" on the TV, then answer the checklist: which apps you use, the dock size and app order, whether to keep the voice assistant, Chromecast and updates. | The assistant backs up, debloats, builds and installs the launcher, and checks each step with screenshots pulled from the TV. With this repo as context it takes about fifteen minutes. ## What you get A home screen that looks like an Apple TV and gets out of the way: | Part | What it looks like | |---|---| | **A pitch-black home** | A dock of your four favourite apps in a rounded band, where Apple TV puts it. | | **A top shelf** | Names the focused app in large type, with an ambient glow in a colour taken from its artwork. | | **The rest of your apps in a grid** | Slides up when you press Down. | | **One floating glass highlight** | Springs from tile to tile. The focused tile lifts and shows its name. | | **Three frosted buttons** | Inputs (HDMI ports under the names you gave them in the TV's settings, AV, Live TV), Wi-Fi or Ethernet with the network name, Settings. | | **A greeting, a thin clock and the date** | In [Outfit](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Outfit), and a matching Clock screensaver. Set `show_stats` in config or a theme for one line under the clock: CPU, free memory and free storage. It stays off unless you turn it on, and it refreshes only while Home is on screen. | | **Themes and module cards** | Themes change colours, wallpaper, dock and columns without a rebuild, and module cards let other apps plug a tile in, only with your say-so. | And a TV that stops working against you: no sponsored rows, no "Discover" nags, no analytics phoning home, no apps you never asked for. | | | |---|---| | ![The top shelf names the focused app over an ambient glow in its colour](docs/focus-2-up-netflix.png) | ![The Inputs popup: HDMI ports with what is connected, AV and Live TV](docs/inputs-menu.jpg) | | *Top shelf and ambient glow* | *Inputs: HDMI with connection state, AV, Live TV* | | ![The grid with the glass highlight on a tile and its name beneath](docs/focus-1-fancode.png) | ![The Clock screensaver: a thin clock drifting over the glow](docs/clock-screensaver.png) | | *The grid, one glass highlight, the tile's name* | *Clock screensaver, drifts so nothing burns in* | | ![The aurora theme: a wallpaper and tinted pills, pushed without a rebuild](themes/aurora/screenshot.jpg) | ![Six columns and a six-app dock from a theme's config.json](themes/six-columns/screenshot.jpg) | | *Aurora theme, pushed with `tools/theme.sh`* | *Six columns and a six-app dock, same launcher* | ## Supported TVs Anything running **Android TV** or **Google TV**. | Platform | What works | |---|---| | **Android TV, Google TV** | The debloat and the launcher. | | **Fire TV** | The debloat half only, since Fire OS will not hand Home to a third-party launcher. And on the 2015 Fire TV Box (Fire OS 5) even that half fails: every `pm` route is refused. | | **A few China-market TCL sets** | They refuse to install any launcher at all; their lists say so in the header. | | **Samsung (Tizen), LG (webOS)** | Different systems. See [SHOWCASE.md](SHOWCASE.md#other-platforms-fire-tv-and-lg-webos) for two webOS ports, and [docs/devices/samsung-tizen.md](docs/devices/samsung-tizen.md) for what a 2021 Samsung set answers over Wi-Fi (no ADB, so no `pm disable-user`) if you are weighing a Tizen port. | Tested lists from contributors, one folder per model in [`examples/`](examples/): **TCL** 50 · **Xiaomi** 26 · **Sony** 23 · **Philips** 12 · **Hisense** 8 · **Skyworth** 8 · **Amazon Fire TV** 7 · **Thomson** 4 · **Google** 3 · **Panasonic** 3 · **BenQ** 2 · **CHiQ** 2 · **FFalcon** 2 · **Haier** 2 · **Hitachi** 2 · **Kalley** 2 · **Nokia** 2 · **NVIDIA Shield** 2 · **OnePlus** 2 · **onn** 2 · **Redmi** 2 · **Toshiba** 2 · **Vu** 2 · AiPro2K · AIWA · Artel · Caxium · Cecotec · Challenger · Compac · Dialog · EKO · Freebox · Insignia Fire TV · JVC · Karbonn · Kogan · Motorola · MTC · Noblex · OK. · PEAQ · Polytron · PRISM+ · RCA · Sankey · SANYO · SHARP · Super General · Tele System · Tornado · Verizon · Vidda · Vision · Anker Nebula, BYINTEK, Epson, Gadnic, JMGO, Portronics, Stellamore, Wanbo and XGIMI projectors

Your TV not here? The prompt discovers the bloat itself. Add your list afterwards and the next person with your model skips that step: [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). ## Doing it by hand Everything the assistant does, you can run yourself. The tools need Python 3 and nothing else. ```bash python3 -m venv tools/venv && tools/venv/bin/pip install -r tools/requirements.txt export TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 # your TV's IP address tools/venv/bin/python -I tools/tv.py --probe # model, Android version, firmware tools/venv/bin/python -I tools/tv.py 'pm list packages' # one shell command on the TV tools/disable.sh examples/xiaomi-mi-tv-4a/debloat.txt # apply a debloat list tools/restore.sh examples/xiaomi-mi-tv-4a/debloat.txt # undo it, stock launcher back tools/venv/bin/python -I tools/check.py examples/xiaomi-mi-tv-4a/debloat.txt # what a firmware update undid TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 launcher/build-and-install.sh # build the launcher and make it Home tools/theme.sh themes/aurora # push a theme; --reset removes it ``` | Tool | What it does | |---|---| | [`tools/tv.py`](tools/tv.py) | Pure-Python ADB client: shell, batch, push, pull, and screenshots, optionally pressing remote keys first. Works where the stock `adb` binary is blocked. | | [`tools/b64push.py`](tools/b64push.py) | Uploads large files such as APKs in base64 chunks and verifies the checksum. | | [`tools/relay.py`](tools/relay.py) | Forwards a local port to the TV's ADB port, for assistants whose sandbox can't reach your network. Listens on this computer only. [Guide](tools/relay.md). | | [`tools/disable.sh`](tools/disable.sh), [`restore.sh`](tools/restore.sh) | Apply or undo a debloat list, the undo from the state recorded before the change. | | [`tools/recovery.py`](tools/recovery.py) | Writes the record `disable.sh` needs to undo itself, and prints the restore batch. | | [`tools/check.py`](tools/check.py) | Compares the TV with the list that was applied, for what a firmware update undid; `--fix` puts it back. | | [`tools/privacy.py`](tools/privacy.py) | Audits the TV for voice, ACR and telemetry candidates and prints the evidence for each; `--write` turns the findings into a list `disable.sh` and `restore.sh` already understand. | | [`tools/theme.sh`](tools/theme.sh) | Push a folder from [`themes/`](themes/) to the launcher and restart Home. | | [`tools/race_calendar.py`](tools/race_calendar.py) | Writes this season's F1 calendar into a theme for race-weekend mode, from the free Jolpica API. | | [`launcher/build-and-install.sh`](launcher/build-and-install.sh) | Builds a shrunk release (about 445 KB), installs it, switches Home, and rolls back if Home does not land on it. | The scripts never leave the TV without a Home app: they only disable a stock launcher they recognise, and skip the Home app in a list until another launcher answers HOME. Details below.
Windows (PowerShell) Every script has a PowerShell twin next to it. On Windows with Android Studio installed nothing else is needed: ```powershell python -m venv tools\venv; tools\venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r tools\requirements.txt powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File launcher\build-and-install.ps1 -TvHost 192.168.1.50 powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File tools\disable.ps1 -TvHost 192.168.1.50 examples\xiaomi-mi-tv-4a\debloat.txt ```
How the scripts protect Home The install scripts ask the TV which launcher owns Home and only disable one they recognise (`tvlauncher` or `launcherx`); pass `STOCK_LAUNCHER=` (`-StockLauncher`) to override, or `none` to leave it alone. `tools/disable.sh` (`disable.ps1`) applies the same rule before it disables anything: if the list contains the app that owns Home and no other app on the TV answers HOME, it skips that entry, says why, and disables the rest of the list. The setup wizard, the settings apps, a vendor `FallbackHome` and factory-test apps (Xiaomi's `com.duokan.factorytest`) answer HOME too and don't count. So a list applied before the launcher handover cannot leave the TV with nothing to start. Run the same list again once `launcher/build-and-install.sh` has made the new launcher Home and the entry is applied; `FORCE_HOME=1` (`$env:FORCE_HOME`) disables it anyway.
Where your lists can live Debloat list paths passed to `disable.sh` and `restore.sh` are relative to the directory you run from, so your own lists can live outside the repository. Absolute paths also work.
## The microphone, and what can be said about it "Which of these packages is listening?" has no honest one-line answer, and a permission scan makes it worse: on many sets most packages run as `android.uid.system`, so fifty of them show `RECORD_AUDIO: granted=true` and none of them record anything. On others the microphone is in the remote, not the panel, and a package with no audio permission at all still sees everything on screen — ACR clients such as `tv.inscape.tvclient.inscapeacr` identify content from the picture and need only `INTERNET`. `tools/privacy.py` reports what the TV actually says instead of guessing: `TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/venv/bin/python -I tools/privacy.py` prints voice, ACR and telemetry candidates in three groups, each with its evidence — named by the firmware's own `voice_interaction_service`, a known component from [`examples/`](examples/), or nothing but a matching name — plus whether the package declares `RECORD_AUDIO`, whether it shares the system UID, and whether `appops` shows the microphone op was ever used since boot. `--write privacy.txt` turns the identified candidates into a normal debloat list, so applying it and undoing it are the commands you already use (`tools/disable.sh`, `tools/restore.sh`). Packages that only matched by name stay out unless you pass `--include-low`; they are the ones to check with `dumpsys package ` first. What the audit cannot do is prove intent. `appops` shows an op was touched, not what happened to the stream afterwards, and no scan of package names proves a TV is or is not recording. Disabling an assistant is a trade you make with a specific loss (the remote's mic button, voice search inside apps), which is why the report names that loss per package instead of calling it a win. ## The launcher A small native home screen for Android TV: **about 445 KB**, plain Java, built for TVs with 1 GB of RAM. No blur, no video, no network permission, no background services. The **TV** needs Android 8.0 (API 26) or newer: `minSdk` is a compile-time floor in [`launcher/app/build.gradle`](launcher/app/build.gradle), and the install script asks the TV for `ro.build.version.sdk` before it builds, so an older set is told both numbers instead of failing at `pm install` (see [Troubleshooting](docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md) for what is left on such a set). | What | How it works | |---|---| | **Configure** | Dock order, hidden apps, Live TV app, 4 to 7 tiles per row, reduced motion. All in [`config.xml`](launcher/app/src/main/res/values/config.xml) | | **Settings on the TV** | Hold OK on the Settings pill for Launcher settings: tiles per row, animations, advanced effects | | **Themes** | Background, wallpaper and layout from a `config.json` pushed over Wi-Fi, no rebuild. Five ship in [`themes/`](themes/) | | **24 languages** | Follows the TV's language, with a fully mirrored right-to-left layout for Hebrew | | **App library** | Optional: browse every installed app and add or remove Home shortcuts. See [the app library guide](docs/app-library.md) | | **Module cards** | Any TV app can offer its own tile; you approve each one once. See [`docs/modules.md`](docs/modules.md) | | **Add-ons** | Optional apps that plug in as module cards, kept in [`addons/`](addons/) and never built into the launcher | | **Clock screensaver** | A drifting clock over the glow, so nothing burns in | | **Remote keys** | Keeps the Input, YouTube and gear buttons working after the stock launcher is gone |
Build it yourself It needs JDK 17 and Android SDK platform 34. On macOS: `brew install openjdk@17 android-commandlinetools` and `sdkmanager "platforms;android-34" "build-tools;34.0.0"`. On Linux the install script finds `~/Android/Sdk` and the `java` on your PATH.
Configure [`config.xml`](launcher/app/src/main/res/values/config.xml) sets the dock order, hidden apps, the Live TV package, columns (tiles shrink from 5 up), rows under the dock, an optional VPN app for the network pill, and `reduced_motion` for TVs whose GPU cannot keep up. Themes set the same keys plus a background colour and a wallpaper.
Launcher settings and the default home - Click **Settings** for the TV's own settings. Hold OK on it and choose **Launcher settings** to set 4, 5, 6 or 7 apps per row, turn animations on or off, and opt into advanced effects (tile lift, icon zoom and smooth ambient-colour transitions; they may use more memory). - **Follow theme** clears the on-TV choices. Pushing or resetting a theme clears them too. - **Change the default home:** Launcher settings and the optional Default-home tile (`show_home_settings_shortcut`) open Android's home picker. Choose the original launcher to stop using CleanYourTV as Home, or CleanYourTV to return. The original launcher must be enabled; if the install script disabled it, run the restore script below first. Some TVs provide no home picker.
Languages English, German, Spanish, Catalan, French, Russian, Serbian (Latin), Polish, Czech, Italian, Portuguese, Turkish, Arabic, Hebrew, Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese (Taiwan), Thai, Finnish, Vietnamese, Bangla, Indonesian, Norwegian Bokmål, Dutch and Uzbek (Latin). The launcher follows the TV's language. Android 13+ can set it for the launcher alone: `tools/tv.py 'cmd locale set-app-locales com.gathin.tvhome --locales ca'`. Hebrew mirrors the layout: menu buttons on the left, date and clock on the right with the greeting above, dock and app rows starting on the right with matching remote navigation, the input selector's icons and labels on the right, and dates with the month prefix ב (for example, 19 באוקטובר). The Clock screensaver right-aligns its date and time. Russian covers every screen, including race weekends, festival greetings and the Shamsi date. Other languages keep their original layouts.
Module cards Any TV app can declare its own tile (label, caption, glow). The launcher asks you once per app, keeps it hidden by default, and remembers the answer for that app's signing key and card name. Hold OK on Settings and choose Module cards to change your mind. How to make one: [`docs/modules.md`](docs/modules.md); the contract: [`docs/specs/card.md`](docs/specs/card.md).
Clock screensaver Pick "Clock" in the TV's screensaver settings, or over ADB: ```bash tools/tv.py 'settings put secure screensaver_components com.gathin.tvhome/.ClockDream; settings put secure screensaver_enabled 1' ```
Remote keys - An optional accessibility service keeps the remote's **Input** button working on Google TV (`INPUT_KEY_SERVICE=1` at install). - It can bring back other buttons only the stock launcher answered, such as the **YouTube** button (`app_keys` and `input_key_keycodes`, in config.xml or a theme; `HOME_KEY_SERVICE=1` reads `app_keys` too). - A `hold:` prefix on an `app_keys` entry gives that button a second app: a normal press opens the unprefixed app, holding for half a second opens the hold one (by keycode or `hold:scan:...`). - `HOME_KEY_SERVICE=1` also fixes sticks whose Home key sends ALL_APPS, and opens Settings from the remote's **gear** button, even one Android does not map (scancodes or keycodes in config.xml). - With `settings_key_panel` the gear opens a [small quick settings panel](docs/quick-settings-panel.jpg) over Home or any app: TV settings, Display, Network, Apps and Launcher settings.
Navigation and artwork Up and Down move one row. The top buttons never fall through to tiles, and Down from them returns to the dock tile you came from. The last focused app is remembered, and installing or removing an app refreshes the tiles while Home is open. App banners load at xhdpi or better, so low-density TV UIs do not downsample them before the focus zoom.
## Restoring your TV Keep the list you applied. One line puts the TV back the way it was: ```bash TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/restore.sh examples//debloat.txt # Android TV TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/restore.sh examples//debloat.txt com.google.android.apps.tv.launcherx # Google TV ``` | What | How | |---|---| | **A record comes first** | Before `tools/disable.sh` changes anything it writes down what the TV looked like, in `~/.cleanyourtv/`. | | **Restore replays it** | A package you had disabled yourself stays disabled, and Home goes back to the component that owned it. | | **The launcher stays installed** | Remove it from the TV's Settings → Apps if you want it gone. | | **No computer?** | If the TV is unreachable, its own Settings → Apps page can re-enable packages too. |
What the record holds, and what happens without one Before `tools/disable.sh` changes anything it writes down what the TV looked like: for every package in the list whether it was enabled, already disabled or not installed, which component owned Home, and the three animation scales. That record lives in `~/.cleanyourtv/`, one file per TV and list, and a second run of the same list keeps the first record instead of saving the cleaned-up state over it. If you added packages to the list since, that run adds them to the record before disabling them. Keep the list you applied. The restore script replays the record, so a package you had disabled yourself stays disabled and Home goes back to the component that owned it: The `stock launcher` argument is only a fallback: with a record, the launcher that actually owned Home is the one that gets it back, and the argument is used only when nothing answered HOME at the time or this project's launcher owned it. The stock launcher is enabled again either way, unless it was already disabled when the record was taken. Without a record (an older run, or a record you deleted) the script says so and falls back to enabling the whole list and resetting the scales to `1.0`, which is what it used to do. It leaves the new launcher installed (remove it from the TV's Settings → Apps if you want it gone) and does not know about packages you disabled outside the list. To switch back later, run the install script again; it works out which launcher to disable even when Home has fallen back to Android's chooser. If the TV is unreachable, its own Settings → Apps page can re-enable packages too.
## After a firmware update An update installs over the cleaned-up system: the listed packages come back, Home goes to the stock launcher, and new preloads appear that no list mentions. Nothing else here notices, so compare the TV with the list you applied: ```bash TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/venv/bin/python -I tools/check.py examples//debloat.txt ``` It prints what drifted and exits 1 when anything did, so a weekly job on a home server or a Pi is enough to hear about it: ```bash 0 9 * * 1 cd ~/cleanyourtv && TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/venv/bin/python -I tools/check.py examples//debloat.txt ``` `--fix` reapplies the list to what drifted: it switches Home to the launcher the list does not disable (pass a package as the second argument if you run a fork), then disables the listed packages that came back, and reads the TV back to confirm both. It writes no recovery record, because the record already holds the state from before the first run: `tools/restore.sh` still returns the TV to stock afterwards. Home is fixed first; if no launcher is left to take it, `--fix` changes nothing and says so. It runs the same safety checks as `tools/disable.sh` before it disables anything, since an update is the moment they matter again: it leaves setupwraith on while the saved Wi-Fi network belongs to it (`FORCE_SETUPWRAITH=1` on Ethernet), leaves the packages under the HDMI/AV inputs on (`TVINPUT_ALLOW=1` if you really want them off), and never takes Home to a vendor `FallbackHome` or a factory-test app. Each package it leaves on comes with the reason and exits 1, because the TV is not back to the list until you deal with that one by hand. Lists that also disable the updater get no updates at all. To install one, re-enable the updater on the TV, let it update, run `check.py --fix`, and disable the updater again. On Windows the same command is `tools\venv\Scripts\python.exe -I tools\check.py `. ## When something goes wrong The full list of things that bit us is in [docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md](docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md). The three that matter most: - 🍎 **macOS blocks `adb connect`** ("No route to host") under Local Network privacy. `tools/tv.py` avoids the binary. - ⚠️ **Disable the stock launcher only after the new one is installed and running**, or Home lands on a factory test app. The install script orders this for you. - 🔁 **On Google TV the setup wizard** (`com.google.android.tungsten.setupwraith`) can take Home and crash-loop the system after the stock launcher is disabled. Disable it too, and list it in your `debloat.txt` so restore brings it back. But check `dumpsys wifi | grep -o 'cname=[^ ]*'` first: if the Wi-Fi network was saved during setup it belongs to setupwraith, and disabling it deletes the network (re-join it in Settings first; `tools/disable.sh` skips setupwraith until you do). On Google's own Chromecast and on the Google TV Streamer it also costs phone casting, see [Troubleshooting](docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md). Stuck already? `tools/tv.py 'pm enable --user 0 com.google.android.apps.tv.launcherx'`. ## Questions people ask
Is this safe? Can it brick the TV? Nothing is flashed, rooted or deleted; packages are disabled in the user profile. The risk is disabling something the TV leans on, which is why lists are applied in small batches with a restore script ready. The TV's own Settings → Apps page can re-enable packages even without the tools.
What about firmware updates? Most lists disable the update service, so updates arrive only when you re-enable it. If one lands, the worst case is a package coming back and you re-run the script.
Won't the apps break? Streaming apps still update through the Play Store, which is left alone. The launcher just lists what is installed and launches it with intents that have been stable for a decade.
Can I do this for someone in another home? Yes, over a private [Tailscale](https://tailscale.com) link instead of the same Wi-Fi: either Tailscale on their TV, shared with you, or a computer or Apple TV at their home routing to it. Never by opening the ADB port on their router. Step by step in [docs/REMOTE.md](docs/REMOTE.md).
Isn't ADB access a security hole? It is one explicit "allow this computer" tap on the TV, the same as developing an Android app. Network ADB is plaintext on port 5555, and on firmware with `ro.adb.secure=0` any device on the LAN gets a shell, so close it when you are done: 1. On the TV: Developer options → turn **USB debugging** and **Network/ADB debugging** off, and revoke the USB debugging authorisations. 2. Reboot the TV, then confirm the port is gone from your computer: `python3 tools/adb-closed.py ` must say the port is closed. With `nc -vz 5555`, only "Connection refused" counts: on macOS, Local Network privacy can block `nc` and make it fail with "No route to host" even while the port is open. The launcher keeps working without debugging.
Can it block ads inside apps too? Partly, with Android's Private DNS (Android 9 and newer). Point it at an ad-blocking resolver such as [AdGuard DNS](https://adguard-dns.io) and every app's ad and tracker domains stop resolving, system-wide, surviving reboots. The trade-off: that resolver then sees every DNS query the TV makes. ```bash tools/tv.py 'settings put global private_dns_specifier dns.adguard-dns.com' tools/tv.py 'settings put global private_dns_mode hostname' ``` It does not remove YouTube ads, which come from the same servers as the videos. If an app stops playing or the TV reports "No internet" (the resolver is down or unreachable), switch back with `tools/tv.py 'settings put global private_dns_mode opportunistic'`.
AirPlay? Not from this repo. Chromecast built-in stays for Android phones. For iPhones, [jqssun/android-airplay-server](https://github.com/jqssun/android-airplay-server) works; an install script for it is in [PR #84](https://github.com/Gathin23/cleanyourtv/pull/84).
Can I just download the APK? Build it with the one-line script; it takes a minute and you control what goes on your TV. No prebuilt binaries.
## Contributing The most useful contribution is your TV's debloat list, so the next person with that model does not have to rediscover it. [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) has the format and the testing we ask for. | How to help | What it means | |---|---| | **Your TV's debloat list** | The most useful one: the next person with that model skips the discovery. | | **Launcher and prompt** | Launcher improvements and sharper prompt wording are welcome too. | | **Built something on top?** | A launcher, a port, a theme: add it to [SHOWCASE.md](SHOWCASE.md), where forty-four projects already live, sorted into home screens, forks, add-ons, tools and other platforms, with an index by TV brand. | The people whose work is in this repo:
Star history
## Contact | For | Where | |---|---| | **Questions about your TV** | [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/Gathin23/cleanyourtv/discussions) | | **Press and partnerships** | [hello@itsgathin.com](mailto:hello@itsgathin.com) | | **Security issues** | Report them privately through the [Security tab](https://github.com/Gathin23/cleanyourtv/security), see [`SECURITY.md`](SECURITY.md) | ## Licence MIT, see [`LICENSE`](LICENSE). # D2R Mobile **An open-source iOS / macOS compatibility layer for Diablo II: Resurrected with the Reign of the Warlock expansion.** It brings the Nintendo Switch release you bought, expansion included, to iPhone, iPad and Mac in full: the original game code runs natively, every control is rebuilt for touch, the frame rate holds at 60 fps, and you are in a game one second after the main menu. There is now a native macOS version as well (first version): on an Apple silicon Mac it starts on double-click and works with keyboard, mouse and gamepad. Apple TV 4K (3rd generation, A15) has a community port (developer preview) that has reached the character-selection screen only on its author's device; see the device table below. This is not a tech demo that "sort of runs". It is a mobile version polished for daily play, from your first character all the way through the endgame. Platforms: iPhone / iPad (iOS 26 and later; iOS 18 – 25 with the older-API build) · Mac (Apple silicon, macOS 26 or later; macOS 15 – 25 with the older-API build) · Apple TV 4K (3rd generation, A15; community port, developer preview) · Game version: Switch release with Reign of the Warlock, 1.0.34.0 (corresponds to PC version 3.3.94012) · English / 中文 / Español / Русский · License: MIT · **Bring your own game files** 中文: [README.zh-CN.md](README.zh-CN.md) · Español: [README.es.md](README.es.md)

| 100% | 60 fps | about 1 s | about 3.8 W | |:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:| | The original gameplay, because it is the original program | Steady, with no drops once the device warms up | From the main menu into a game | Whole-device power draw at 60 fps | ## What it is, and what it is not **It is:** - The game's own aarch64 program, **executing directly on the device**, with no emulated CPU. iPhone and Switch use the same class of processor; only the handful of instructions that cannot run unchanged under Apple's kernel are rewritten, and every other byte of the program is left exactly as shipped. Every class, every Runeword, Terror Zones, bosses, drop rules and quest flow are identical to the original. - The platform services the game expects — system calls, the file system, the graphics API, audio, input — provided by a small host written for Apple platforms. The graphics API is reimplemented entirely on Apple's Metal with no emulation layer in between, and the shaders are translated offline from the game's originals. - A port built for phones, and taken all the way: a complete touch control scheme, edge-to-edge iPhone and true full-screen iPad display, controller support, a power saver mode, save sync, English and Chinese, and a whole set of endgame modes and quality-of-life features the original never had. **It is not:** - An emulator, cloud gaming, or streaming. - **A source of game content. It contains none and distributes none.** There is no game program, art, text, data table or shader in this repository; all of that is generated on your own machine from your own files (see [docs/GAME_FILES.md](docs/GAME_FILES.md)). What the repository does carry is the interface information we recorded to make the port work — shader interface descriptions, the graphics API function table, addresses inside the program and the like — listed item by item in [docs/DERIVED.md](docs/DERIVED.md). - Online. There is no multiplayer; the game runs fully offline and needs no online account. ## Battle-tested All **44** iPhones and iPads in the closed beta — 35 devices registered for direct install (25 iPhones and 10 iPads), plus 9 TestFlight accounts with one device each — **completed Normal, Nightmare and Hell with multiple characters**, and the experience was excellent. From an iPhone 14 Pro Max with 6 GB of memory to the latest iPad Pro, not one device fell behind. | | Models | |---|---| | iPhone | 14 Pro Max, 15, 15 Pro, 15 Pro Max, 16 Plus, 16 Pro, 16 Pro Max, 17 Pro Max and more | | iPad | iPad Air, iPad mini, iPad Pro 11-inch and 12.9 / 13-inch (including M2 and M4) and more | | Lowest model tested | **iPhone 14 Pro Max (A16, 6 GB): a flawless 60 fps** | iPhone and iPad share a single install package.

## Fast, smooth, and easy on the battery Measured on a real device (iPhone 17 Pro Max): | Item | Reading | |---|---| | In-game frame rate | **60 fps**, steady, with no drops once the device warms up | | App launch | 0.15 s | | To the main menu | about 1 s | | From the main menu into a game | **about 1 s** | | Quick Restart, back in a game | about 1.2 s | | Longest frame when changing acts | about 0.1 s | | Whole-device power, 60 fps | **about 3.8 W** (in camp, 50% brightness): nearly 5 hours of continuous play on a full charge | | Whole-device power, power saver mode at 30 fps | **about 1.85 W**, about half the 60 fps figure, for about twice the battery life | Measurement conditions: power is whole-device power measured on 2026-10-10 on an iPhone 17 Pro Max, standing in the Act I camp at 50% brightness, with 60 fps and power saver mode measured in the same scene; battery life is calculated from the measured power and the battery capacity, not by playing from full to empty. Launch and game-entry times were measured on the same model in 2026-10; frame rate and act-change readings were taken on the same model on 2026-10-12 while moving through areas and changing acts after entering a game. The install package is only a little over 100 MB. The game resources (about 5.6 GB) are placed on the phone separately, and updating the app touches neither your saves nor the resources. Why it is this fast: the program executes natively, and not a single instruction goes through emulation; graphics go straight to Metal; every shader is translated offline and compiled ahead of time, so nothing is compiled when you enter a new scene. Older chips (A16 and earlier, such as the iPhone 14 family and iPhone 15) do not support the game's original compressed texture format; they need an extra texture pack made from your own game files, and then run at full frame rate too — see [docs/LEGACY_DEVICES.md](docs/LEGACY_DEVICES.md). ## Redesigned for fingers This is not a gamepad pasted onto the screen. Every panel and every action was rebuilt for fingers under one design principle: **keep the original interface language, and use gestures instead of adding buttons to the screen**. Text sizes and tap targets are sized for fingers. You know how to play the moment you pick it up, and it stays comfortable over long sessions.

- **Move**: a virtual stick with precise diagonals; tap an NPC or the ground to path there automatically; doors, portals and cave entrances are tappable across their whole surface. - **Fight**: press a skill button to cast, hold to keep casting, **drag to aim at any angle**; nearby monsters are targeted automatically. Two skill sets. Skills on your secondary weapons cast with one tap — the game swaps weapons, casts, and swaps back — and the button shows the charges remaining. - **Boss health bar**: pinned to the top of the screen, showing the percentage remaining. - **Items**: tap, double-tap, long-press and drag and drop all track your finger. Double-tap gear to equip or unequip it; drag an item anywhere onto the vendor panel to sell it; on a stack, double-tap takes 1 and long-press takes 3; long-press an empty inventory slot to sort everything. - **Text**: typed with the system keyboard. Character names can be in Chinese; leave the name blank for a random one. - **Screen**: on iPhone the 19.5:9 display is filled edge to edge, clear of the notch and rounded corners; on iPad the game fills the entire screen, and the interface centers itself when you open a panel; the 3D picture can be brightened. ### Controller Connect a controller and press any button: the interface switches to the original controller layout, with button prompts at the bottom of every panel. Touch the screen and you are back in the touch interface instantly. Inventory, stash, skill tree, Chronicle and settings are fully controller-navigable, with the same button mapping as on Switch.

## New ways to play, on top of the original Finishing the original game is only the beginning. Without touching the original rules, we added a full set of endgame content that keeps you farming. ### Greater Rift Enter through the red portal in Harrogath after completing Hell. There are 100 levels, and the monsters grow stronger with each one; fill the progress bar and slay the Rift Guardian within 15 minutes to clear a level. Every 2 levels cleared grants +1 Skill Point and +5 Stat Points, and the skill level cap rises from 20 to 40. Every 10 levels has a first-clear reward, and clearing level 10 unlocks six new equipment slots for your mercenary.

### Endgame Boss Rush, Elysium mode, and the Kill Board - **Endgame Boss Rush**: unlocks after completing Hell, with 12 stages; stage 11 is Diablo Clone, and stage 12 is the three Uber bosses. - **Elysium mode** (chosen at character creation): Unique ×5, Set ×3, Runes ×5; the "no drop" chance is cut to a tenth, and bosses always drop as on a first kill. - **Kill Board**: for every boss, the number of kills, the time of the first kill, how many Unique and Set items it has dropped, and your best and average kill times.

### Storage: a collector's paradise - **Chronicle stash**: every identified Unique and Set item has its own fixed slot, shared by all characters, searchable, with deposit and withdraw; the Deposit button sends the Unique and Set items in your inventory and Horadric Cube there in one tap. - **Stash**: widened to 14 columns, with 5 personal pages and 5 shared pages. - **Trove**: the gem, rune and material pages merged into one, with the Horadric Cube's crafting grid in the middle, so finding things and crafting no longer means flipping between pages. Runes, gems and materials you put into the personal or shared pages are filed here automatically. - **Pouch**: an extended inventory. Runes and gems found in the field go into it automatically and take up no inventory space.

### Effortless farming | | | |---|---| | Auto-recast buffs | Buff skills you have learned do not need a slot on the skill bar: when a buff runs out, it is recast the moment you stand still; buffs that come from your secondary weapons (such as Battle Orders from Call to Arms) swap weapons, recast and swap back on their own | | Potions and belt | Auto-drink has two tiers: a healing potion below 50% Life, a rejuvenation potion below 30%; **your mercenary is fed automatically by the same rule**. Potions on the ground are picked up automatically when the belt has room; double-tap an empty belt slot to refill the whole belt | | Loot filter | From Nightmare on, the original loot filter is switched on automatically to hide clutter: light filtering in Nightmare, heavy in Hell | | Auto-pickup | Low runes and gems go straight into the Pouch; the high ones are left for you to pick up yourself | | Valuable drop alerts | High runes and Unique items raise a light beam and land with a different drop sound; the phone vibrates at one of three strengths — light, medium or heavy — according to value | | Runeword helper | Long-press a socketed base to list the Runewords it can make and their stats; once you have the runes, socket them all in one tap | | Minimap guidance | Every map marks its Waypoint and exits; every quest goal is on the map; when a target is off screen, its name is written along the screen edge | | Chores removed | Free identification, free Town Portal with no scrolls needed, spawning right beside the Waypoint, Quick Restart, refreshable vendor stock | | Saves | Saved immediately when you switch apps, swipe the app away or quit; iCloud sync across devices (requires signing with a paid developer account) | Most features can be toggled one by one in game under Options → Custom.

### English, Chinese, Spanish and Russian The whole game switches between English, Chinese, Spanish and Russian under Options → Custom; after a restart, the interface is in the language you chose. On first launch it follows your device language (Spanish from Spain uses the game's esES text, other Spanish regions use the Latin American esMX text). In English, Spanish and Russian, items, skills and monsters use the original Diablo II wording, and everything we added — Greater Rift, Chronicle, the settings page, gesture prompts, map name plates — is translated too (item notes are translated for Chinese and Spanish only). Russian is the game's single ruRU text, with no regional variants. Voice acting: Chinese UI gets Chinese voices; Russian gets the original Russian voices when your game files include them (a package built from the complete game data does), otherwise English; everything else is English.

## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR G["Your game files
(program + resources)"] --> P["Rewriter
changes only a few instructions"] G --> S["Shader translation
original → Metal"] P --> H["Host
system services"] S --> X["Graphics layer
the graphics API on Metal"] H --> A["iOS app
touch and interface"] X --> A ``` | Part | Where | What it does | |---|---|---| | Program rewriter | `dm/tools/patch_nso.py` | Rewrites only the few instructions that cannot run unchanged under Apple's kernel (thread-pointer registers, system calls, timers) and leaves the rest of the program byte-for-byte as shipped | | Host | `dm/host` | Loads the rewritten program and provides the platform services it calls | | Graphics | `dm/gfx` | Implements the game's graphics API on Metal; shaders are translated offline from the game's originals | | iOS app | `dm/ios` | The app shell, touch controls and interface | | Verification | `dm/verify` | Checks that the rewritten code behaves exactly like the original, plus the regression gates every change goes through | **Why you can trust it:** the stability is not luck. The test and verification tooling is part of the project — unit tests for the host and graphics layers, an equivalence check for every rewritten instruction, scripted walkthrough regression for the touch interface, and on-device smoke tests. Start with `make -C dm/host/tests run`, `make -C dm/gfx/tests run` and `dm/verify/regress.sh` (run them inside the Python environment prepared in step 2 below; `regress.sh` also needs `brew install llvm`). How to contribute is in [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). ## Which devices are supported Minimum: **an A14 / M1 chip or later** — the graphics layer needs Metal 3, which Apple supports from A14 / M1 on (see Apple's [Metal support on Apple devices](https://support.apple.com/102894) and [Metal Feature Set Tables](https://developer.apple.com/metal/Metal-Feature-Set-Tables.pdf)). | Device | Playable? | How | How sure we are | |---|---|---|---| | **iPhone / iPad, A17 Pro and later** (iPhone 15 Pro and later, iPhone 16 and later, iPads with M-series chips) | Yes | iOS 26 or later: the default shell / default build; iOS 18 – 25: the iOS 18 shell / [older-API build](docs/OLDER_SYSTEMS.md) | Main devices, played daily | | **iPhone / iPad, A16 and earlier** (all iPhone 14 models, iPhone 15 / 15 Plus, iPhone 13 series and so on) | Yes, with one extra step | Make a Legacy Device Pack from your own game files as in [docs/LEGACY_DEVICES.md](docs/LEGACY_DEVICES.md) and include it when making the install package; the system split is the same as the row above | Played by players: iPhone 14 Pro Max (A16, 6 GB) at 60 fps; iPhone 13 Pro Max (A15, 6 GB) in the 30 fps mode | | **Devices with 4 GB of RAM** (such as the 6th-generation iPad mini or the 4th-generation iPad Air) | Runs, but memory is very tight (we are still reducing memory use) | Same as the A16-and-earlier row (with the Legacy Device Pack) | Tested by a player: on an iPad mini 6 (A15, 4 GB, iPadOS 27) a few minutes of Act I ran at 50–58 fps after automatic quality reduction, with constant system memory warnings and only about 560 MB below the system memory limit — busy scenes with many monsters and effects may be ended by the system; on an earlier version an iPad Air 4 (A14, 4 GB) was ended by the system a few seconds after launch | | **A14 chips with 6 GB of RAM or more** (such as iPhone 12 Pro / 12 Pro Max) | No reports yet | Same as the A16-and-earlier row | If you have tried, please open an Issue and tell us | | **A13 and earlier chips** (such as the iPhone 11 series and the 2020 iPad Pro) | Not supported | — | The graphics chip does not support Metal 3 (tested by a player on an iPad Pro with A12Z; Apple's references are above the table); the app says so at launch instead of crashing | | **Mac, Apple silicon** | Yes (native macOS App) | macOS 26 or later: the default build; macOS 15 – 25: the [older-API build](docs/OLDER_SYSTEMS.md). Keyboard, mouse and gamepad all work; what each can do is in [docs/MAC.md](docs/MAC.md) | A player has played the older-API build on macOS 15.7.7 | | **Apple TV 4K (3rd generation, A15)** | Community port ([@yinqingyan](https://github.com/yinqingyan), contributed under the MIT License with the author's consent), developer preview | Build as in [dm/tvos/README.md](dm/tvos/README.md) and copy the game files and the Legacy Device Pack into the app; real hardware only, the Simulator cannot run it; saves live in the Caches directory, which the system may purge | Reached the character-selection screen on real hardware; entering the game, full controller mapping and saves are not verified yet, and the maintainers have not tested it on real hardware | | **Intel Macs** | Not supported | — | — | **What the dialogs in the App mean** - **"One More Step for This Device"**: this phone can run the game; the install package was made without the Legacy Device Pack. Make the pack as in [docs/LEGACY_DEVICES.md](docs/LEGACY_DEVICES.md), make the install package again with it and reinstall. - **"Device Not Supported … iPhone 15 Pro and later can play"**: this is the old text from before v1.0.9. You are on an old version; update to the latest. For A16 and earlier devices, then follow the line above. **What a package you build yourself does not have, compared with our test-group builds**: the public version can be built and installed with a free Apple ID. Three things in our test-group builds are not in it: iCloud save sync (the App needs the iCloud signing entitlement, which a self-signed package does not have), downloading packs and resources inside the App, and new-version notices (these two use our own server). The game itself and the features we added are the same. ## Getting started Both routes start with **the files of the game you bought**: the Switch release of Diablo II: Resurrected plus the Reign of the Warlock expansion, updated to 1.0.34.0 (the version the console shows; it corresponds to PC version 3.3.94012, and the directory names and tools in this repository use the latter number). This project is built for the version with that expansion; using it without the expansion is not supported and has not been verified. How to prepare them is in [docs/GAME_FILES.md](docs/GAME_FILES.md). > This project provides only tools and an install shell that contains no game content. We do not distribute or endorse, and are not responsible for, any third party distributing game assets, game executables or install packages that contain game content. Please use only game files you legally own. This project is implemented and verified on the Switch release 1.0.34.0 (which corresponds to PC version 3.3.94012), and by default the tools accept only that version. Community users have reported adapting other versions on their own by following the structure of this repository, and running them successfully. The rule tables are grouped by game version (in `dm/tools/patch_nso.py`, keyed by the build ID of the main program); you are welcome to contribute the version you adapted. **Check your device first**: the "Which devices are supported" table above tells you which build to use and whether you also need a Legacy Device Pack. | | With a Mac | Without a Mac | |---|---|---| | Computer | An Apple silicon Mac with Xcode installed | Windows / Linux / a Mac without Xcode | | Method | A full build from source | Download a "shell" with no game content, use the packaging tool to add your own game content, then install it with a sideloading tool | | Status | The main route; everything above comes from it | Works end to end on Windows, from making the package to playing on a device, and the game program produced on the two systems is byte-for-byte identical; the one step nobody has tried yet is signing with a sideloading tool — try it and tell us | | Instructions | The three steps below | [docs/NO_XCODE.md](docs/NO_XCODE.md) | The Apple account used for signing: a paid developer account gives you everything; a free Apple ID works too (no iCloud save sync, and the app has to be re-signed and reinstalled every 7 days). The full list of dependencies is in [docs/DEPENDENCIES.md](docs/DEPENDENCIES.md). ### With a Mac: three steps 1. Put your game files in the workspace (default `~/dm-work`, or set `DM_ROOT`): ``` ~/dm-work/data/switch/3.3.94012/Update/ExeFS/ main, sdk, subsdk0 ~/dm-work/data/switch/3.3.94012/Update/RomFS/ data/… ``` 2. Prepare the workspace. This checks your tools, rewrites the game program, and translates the game's shaders to Metal. The first run takes a while; later runs skip what is already done. ``` ./setup.sh source ~/dm-work/build/cache/dm/venv/bin/activate # run everything after this inside the Python environment setup prepared; if you changed DM_ROOT, use it in place of ~/dm-work ``` 3. Fill in your signing details and build the app: ``` cp dm/ios/local.env.example dm/ios/local.env # set DM_TEAM_ID and DM_BUNDLE_ID; with a free Apple ID also set DM_FREE_ACCOUNT=1 and DM_IOS_UDID, and keep the phone connected while building cd dm/ios && ./run.sh build # targets both iPhone and iPad by default; for iPhone only: DM_DEVICE_FAMILY=1 ./run.sh build ``` The first time you open the app on your phone, it asks for the "game resource folder" — the 18 resource archives from your game files. Where to put them is in the section "The "game resource folder" that goes on the phone" of [docs/GAME_FILES.md](docs/GAME_FILES.md). `./setup.sh check` is a health check: it reports the state of this computer, the tools, the game files and the signing configuration item by item, and for everything missing it says where to get it and which command to run next; it changes nothing. If what you have is a whole game package (`.xci` / `.nsp`), `./setup.sh ` first extracts the game files into place and then carries on (install hactool first). Run `./setup.sh` again after every update to a new commit: it rebuilds the patched binaries and the shader library for the current sources (steps that are already up to date are skipped). It also rewrites three files in the repository that change with your local tool fingerprints (`dm/gfx/tools/dmsh_chain.lock`, `dm/gfx/nvn/dmsh_chain.h`, `dm/gfx/nvn/c1_full.tsv`); that is expected, do not commit them. ### Playing directly on a Mac After the same `./setup.sh`, one more command builds a native macOS App that starts on double-click and works with keyboard, mouse and gamepad, with no developer account: ```bash source ~/dm-work/build/cache/dm/venv/bin/activate dm/tools/mac_app.sh # macOS 26 or later: produces ~/dm-work/out/macapp/D2R Mobile.app DM_MAC_M3=1 dm/tools/mac_app.sh # macOS 15 – 25: produces D2R Mobile M3.app ``` The interface is the original's gamepad interface. Keyboard: Space confirms, Esc goes back, Return, the `=` key opens the menu / a new character, W A S D moves, and every other gamepad button has a key. Mouse: clicking a monster, NPC or object walks over and interacts, and the skill slots, potion cells and key hints at the bottom, buttons and tabs in panels, the class figures when creating a character and the minimap can all be clicked; clicking empty ground walks there and holding keeps walking, clicking a monster attacks it, and items take double clicks and drags. With a keyboard, the prompts on screen show keyboard keys. Saves stay on this Mac (an App you build yourself has no iCloud sync) and can be imported by hand from an iPhone / iPad. The key table, how to create a character, what the mouse can do, the import steps and the known shortcomings are in [docs/MAC.md](docs/MAC.md). Keyboard and a physical gamepad have not been operated by a person yet — if you try it, please tell us how it went. ### Without a Mac: the shell plus the packaging tool Download our prebuilt "shell" package (`D2RMobile-shell-build-input.zip`; `D2RMobile-shell-ios18-build-input.zip` for iOS 18 – 25), which contains no game content, from this repository's [Releases page](https://github.com/jhaizhou-ops/d2r-mobile/releases), add your own game files, make the install package on Windows or Linux, then sign and install it with a sideloading tool. The shell is build input, not an app to install (installed as is, it only shows a dialog and does not start the game); when you move to a new release, make the install package again with the new shell. On this route only, because the computer making the package has no Apple shader compiler, the **first launch** on the phone spends about 7 minutes compiling shaders (once, with a progress bar); a package built with Xcode has no such step. The steps, and how far each one has been verified, are in [docs/NO_XCODE.md](docs/NO_XCODE.md). ## Known limitations | Item | Status | |---|---| | Online play | Out of scope; fully offline | | `.nsp` / `.xci` game packages | The tools only check the version of the main program and do not distinguish package formats; we ran the whole path with an `.xci` ourselves, and users have reported that `.nsp` packages work perfectly as well | | Signing and installing with a sideloading tool (Sideloadly, AltStore and the like) | Not verified; open an issue and tell us how it went | | Making the package on Linux | Not verified (verified on Windows and Mac) | | Devices that have not moved to iOS 26 / macOS 26 | Playable with the older-API build (minimum iOS 18.0 / macOS 15.0): [docs/OLDER_SYSTEMS.md](docs/OLDER_SYSTEMS.md); the full device table is under "Which devices are supported" above | | A16 and earlier devices (iPhone 14 family, iPhone 15 / 15 Plus and so on) | Playable; they need a Legacy Device Pack and an App built with it: [docs/LEGACY_DEVICES.md](docs/LEGACY_DEVICES.md). "One More Step for This Device" (older versions say "Device Not Supported") in the App means this step is missing | | The "one-line verdict" and "legacy Chinese name" entries in item notes | These two content tables are not shipped with the repository; you can supply your own, see `dm/ios/tools/annot/README.md` | ## Contributing and feedback - If you hit a problem, open an issue (there is a template); attaching the file exported by Share Diagnostics in the pause menu helps the most. - For the items marked not verified, tell us whether they worked or not. Either answer is valuable. - To change the code: get the test entry points above passing first. Every change has to pass the regression gates. **Taking it to other platforms:** this approach is not limited to iPhone and iPad. Apple silicon Macs already have a native version (see "Playing directly on a Mac" above), built from the same game program and the same host; Apple TV also has a community port (developer preview, see the device table). Android phones use the same class of processor, so the game program executes natively there as well, and the route is fully open: the only parts to replace are the sides of the host and the graphics layer that face the platform. The author has no Android phone at hand, and would love to see someone bring it to Android. **Taking it to other games:** someone has already tried other Switch games on the same host. The host has some behaviour that is on by default on iOS and was written for this one game; another game runs into these first, so turn them off or move them out before you start: - `dm/host/hle_oe.c`: the 3D render scale defaults to 0.75 on iOS, and `scale3d_tick` rewrites it at offsets inside this game's renderer — with another game that is a wild pointer. - `dm/host/hle_fs.c`: seeding the shared stash on first launch (`DM_STASH_SEED`) and the touch-layout default settings (`DM_TOUCH_DEFAULTS`) are on by default on iOS. - `dm/host/main.c`: the save-flush throttle patches a constant at a fixed address in the game program; `argv[0]` is hard-coded to `"D2R"`. - `dm/host/hle_time.c`: the fixed-time test switch recognises a fixed address in the game program. - `front_game_res` in `dm/host/front_mac.m`: the docked / handheld resolutions are hard-coded to 1600×900 / 1280×720. - `dm/host/dm_cloudsync.c`: character directories are recognised by `.d2s`. - `dm/host/dm_cursor.c` and `dm/host/dm_world.c`: the whole files are specific to this game. The cleaner arrangement is to move these defaults into per-game configuration and keep the host free of game-specific defaults; pull requests in that direction are welcome. ## Documentation by part | Document | Covers | |---|---| | [dm/README.md](dm/README.md) | How the whole thing works, directory layout, common commands, the host's source files | | [dm/gfx/README.md](dm/gfx/README.md) | The graphics layer and the shader translation chain | | [dm/ios/README.md](dm/ios/README.md) | The iOS shell, building and smoke testing | | [dm/verify/README.md](dm/verify/README.md) | What each verification tool checks and what it needs | | [docs/GAME_FILES.md](docs/GAME_FILES.md) | Game files: which ones you need, how to get them from your own console, where to put them | | [docs/DEPENDENCIES.md](docs/DEPENDENCIES.md) | Dependencies and third-party licenses | | [docs/NO_XCODE.md](docs/NO_XCODE.md) | Building without Xcode and without a Mac | | [docs/MAC.md](docs/MAC.md) | Playing on a Mac: building the macOS App, key mapping, known gaps | | [docs/LEGACY_DEVICES.md](docs/LEGACY_DEVICES.md) | Older devices (A16 and earlier): making the texture pack and putting it on the phone | | [docs/OLDER_SYSTEMS.md](docs/OLDER_SYSTEMS.md) | Older systems (iOS 18 – 25, macOS 15 – 25): building the older-API version and combining it with the Legacy Device Pack | | [docs/qa-rift-pet-life.md](docs/qa-rift-pet-life.md) | Regression checklist for minion life in Greater Rifts (what has been run and what has not; additions welcome) | | [docs/DERIVED.md](docs/DERIVED.md) | Game-related material in this repository: what is here, what is not, and why | ## Legal **You must own the game, including the Reign of the Warlock expansion.** This is an independent, non-commercial project. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Blizzard Entertainment or Nintendo. Diablo and Blizzard Entertainment are trademarks of Blizzard Entertainment, Inc.; Nintendo Switch is a trademark of Nintendo. Use it only with a copy of the game that you own. ## Acknowledgements This project stands on the open-source work below. Thank you to its authors and maintainers. - **Ryujinx** (Ryubing 1.3.2, MIT): `dm/third_party/ryujinx` bundles its shader translator unchanged (the Ryujinx.Graphics.Shader, Spv.Generator and Ryujinx.Common projects), which translates the Switch game's shaders to SPIR-V. During development we also ran the original game in a patched Ryujinx as the reference for comparing pictures and game state (see [dm/verify/README.md](dm/verify/README.md); the scripts that build and drive it are not in this repository). - **deko3d** (devkitPro, zlib): the texture layout size algorithm in `dm/gfx/nvn/nvn_tex.c` is ported from it. - **nvn.h** (h1k421, MIT): the graphics API declarations in `dm/gfx/nvn/include/nvn.h`. - **libdeflate** (Eric Biggers, MIT): decompressing game data. - **bcdec** (iOrange, MIT or Unlicense): decoding BC textures on devices that do not support the BC formats. - **FLIP** (NVIDIA, BSD 3-Clause): the image difference metric used in image-quality checks. - **Offline fix patch** (LFS Mod Offline Fix): the 7 rewrites in `dm/tools/patch_nso.py` that let the game run offline come from this community patch. We have no reliable record of where it was first published or who wrote it; if you know, please open an Issue. - Tools used to build and verify: SPIRV-Cross (SPIR-V to Metal Shading Language), XcodeGen, .NET, Capstone and Unicorn (disassembly and equivalence checks of the rewrites), Pillow, numpy, lz4, astcenc (the Legacy Device Pack), hactool (extracting files from a game package), libimobiledevice and LLVM. Versions and links are in [docs/DEPENDENCIES.md](docs/DEPENDENCIES.md). - Community contributions: Joe Hu reported and diagnosed several Greater Rift issues and proposed a verification matrix; seedds found and diagnosed the render-target view format issue on another port (#36). Both are credited as co-authors on the corresponding commits. ## License MIT, see [LICENSE](LICENSE). Third-party code keeps its own license in its own directory; see [docs/DEPENDENCIES.md](docs/DEPENDENCIES.md).

# MacNativeGames

# English

**Breath of the Wild 1.6.0 is now officially supported on Mac!** (Mac only for now: no iPhone or iPad build yet.)
**Tears of the Kingdom 1.0.0, 1.2.1 and 1.4.3 are now officially supported on Mac, iPhone and iPad!**

> **Use your AI assistant to help you build the Mac app. We recommend Claude Code, Codex, or any other AI assistant you prefer.**

[English](#english) | [中文](#chinese)

## Legal

**You must own the game.** Use this project only with a copy of The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom that you bought, and with keys and system files dumped from your own Nintendo Switch. This is an independent, non-commercial project. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Nintendo. The Legend of Zelda and Nintendo Switch are trademarks of Nintendo.

The repository contains no game content and distributes none: no game program, art, text, audio, shaders or keys. Everything the game needs is made on your own computer from your own files when you build the app. The app you build contains the game, so it is for your own use only; do not share it. What the repository does hold is the information needed to make the port work: the patch code, the addresses and hashes used to check your files, and the [shared shader list](docs/shader-list.md), which names shaders and bind states but contains no shader code.

Play your own copy of **The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom** natively on Apple silicon Mac, iPhone, and iPad. Bring your game file (XCI or NSP) and your `prod.keys`; one script builds a Mac app or an unsigned iPhone/iPad IPA. The iOS build requires iOS/iPadOS 26 and iPhone 14 or newer. It is not an emulator: the game's own ARM64 code runs directly on Apple chips (rewritten where the operating system requires it), the Switch system services are answered by a small host, and the game's NVN graphics are rebuilt on Metal. Nothing from the game is in this repository, and the project is not affiliated with Nintendo. Version 1.4.3 has been played on an iPhone 14 and an iPad; see [iPhone and iPad](#iphone-and-ipad).

## Local testing

Tested on **MacBook Air M4 and Mac mini M4**. Local testing has collected **8,582 shaders**, with performance at approximately **90 FPS after shader warm-up, reaching 120 FPS in menus**.

Those are earlier local observations, not a stable frame-rate promise for every version or scene. Version 1.4.3 measurements and compilation stalls are recorded separately in [the test notes](docs/v1.4.3-port.md).

Shaders are automatically collected, compiled and cached as you play. Returning to previously visited scenes typically brings noticeable improvements in frame rates and smoothness because cached shaders can be reused. **8,582 is the number collected so far in local testing, not the game's total shader count or a collection limit**; the cache continues to grow as you explore.

**Shader prewarming on the first launch:** Building the app prepares shaders from your selected game data and includes them in the app: every shader in the game data for its default bind state, plus every variant named in the [shared shader list](docs/shader-list.md). Even with an empty user cache, the first launch imports these shaders. Only what the title screen itself uses is warmed before the first frame (about 2 seconds once macOS has compiled them before); the rest, together with compatible entries in the pipeline manifest, warms in the background behind the title, and the first trip into the world waits up to 15 seconds for it. No preliminary play session or manual cache copy is needed. The current 1.4.3 build prepares 15,266. Building the app also compiles them for your Mac's GPU. With Xcode's Metal toolchain installed they are compiled into the app (about 6 minutes on an M4 for 1.4.3) and work wherever the app goes. Without it they are compiled into macOS's Metal cache (a few minutes), and Metal finds them only while the game runs from where the app was built: if you move the app afterwards (to /Applications, for example), if macOS clears the cache (it does when the system disk fills up), or if another program was using Metal's cache while the app was built (a running game, for example; the build says so), the background warm-up compiles them again, which takes a few minutes, and new scenes can stutter until it finishes. To place the app elsewhere, build it there with `-o`; see [preparation and test details](docs/first-launch-shaders.md). Places no player has reported yet can still need new variants, which the Mac compiles while you play (a short stutter the first time). Playing adds them to your local cache, which is reused on later launches. The game also notes every variant the shared list does not have yet in `shader-list-contribution.txt`, and every 500 of them asks once whether to send the file in a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/ly05010419/MacNativeGames/issues/new?template=shader-list.yml) ("Send" opens the form and shows the file to drag in). It never uploads anything by itself. With git, you can also merge your cache and open a pull request, as [the list's guide](docs/shader-list.md) explains. The list holds shader and pipeline identifiers only, never game data, saves or compiled shaders; every build makes the shaders from the player's own game files.


## What you need

- A Mac with Apple silicon and **macOS 26** or later (the graphics use Metal 4); macOS 27 is supported. 16 GB of memory or more is recommended.
  - Still on macOS 15? A community fork by [1918662410-ship-it](https://github.com/1918662410-ship-it/MacNativeGames) adds a Metal 3 backend for macOS 15. It is maintained there; this repository does not test it.
- About **25 GB** of free disk space for the work folder, in addition to your game file. Keep the output app on the **same APFS volume** to share the large data files through cloning. If cloning is unavailable or the app is on another volume, allow roughly **17 GB more** for the app copy.
- Your Tears of the Kingdom **base game 1.0.0** (`0100F2C0115B6000`) as an **XCI or NSP**, and your `prod.keys`. To build **1.1.2, 1.2.1 or 1.4.3**, supply its separate cumulative update as NSP or NSZ with `--update`; no intermediate update is required. NSZ is decompressed and its NCA hashes are verified before extraction. DLC and combined packages are unsupported.
- For NSP: its common ticket must be included unless the NCAs are rights-free. NSPs do not contain system shared fonts: supply an unpacked firmware NCA directory with `--firmware`, or previously extracted fonts with `--shared-fonts`. The six fonts are checked against this project’s reference dump; a valid BFTTF font from another firmware version is accepted and bound by its own bytes. Valid fonts already in the work folder are reused.

## Build the app

**1. Tools** (once): Xcode command line tools and [Homebrew](https://brew.sh). An internet connection is needed to install build dependencies and fetch pinned sources:

```sh
xcode-select --install
brew install opus libvpx python@3.14
```

For an iPhone/iPad build, install full **Xcode 26 or later** (including the iOS and Metal toolchains), then install the additional tools:

```sh
brew install xcodegen cmake ninja
```

Optional: with Xcode's Metal toolchain (`xcodebuild -downloadComponent MetalToolchain`), the build compiles the startup shaders into the app. It finds an Xcode kept outside `/Applications` too (on another volume, or set `DEVELOPER_DIR`). Without it, the build compiles them into the Mac's own Metal cache for the app's location instead, which does not move with the app: after moving it, the first launch compiles them again.

**2. Download or clone this repository**, then open Terminal in its `MacNativeGames` folder and run the script with your game file and keys:

```sh
python3.14 build_app.py ~/Games/totk.xci -k ~/keys/prod.keys
```

For an NSP, supply the shared fonts too:

```sh
python3.14 build_app.py ~/Games/totk.nsp -k ~/keys/prod.keys --firmware ~/Games/firmware
# Or reuse the six .bfttf files from a previous build:
python3.14 build_app.py ~/Games/totk.nsp -k ~/keys/prod.keys --shared-fonts /path/to/TOTK_build/totk/extracted/firmware/shared-fonts
```

`--firmware` accepts a directory of `.nca` files (unpack a firmware archive first), or an installed firmware `registered` directory. `--shared-fonts` accepts the extracted directory containing `0-standard.bfttf` through `5-nintendo-extension.bfttf`. No fonts or keys are downloaded. For an XCI, fonts are read from its system update partition by default; if that partition is missing, use one of these font options too. By default both input formats produce a macOS `.app`.

To build an unsigned iPhone/iPad IPA instead, add `--platform ios` and use an `.ipa` output path:

```sh
python3.14 build_app.py ~/Games/totk.xci -k ~/keys/prod.keys --platform ios -o ~/Games/TOTK.ipa
```

Add `--update ~/Games/1.4.3.nsp` to select an update, and keep the `--firmware` or `--shared-fonts` option when the base game is an NSP. The first iOS build downloads and compiles device versions of Opus and libvpx and compiles the shader seed for iOS, so it needs an internet connection and substantial temporary disk space (allow at least **45 GB free** for a fresh base build, or **60 GB** for a fresh build with an update). The resulting IPA is unsigned: sign and install it with your sideloading tool, keeping its entitlements (it uses the increased memory limit). iOS/iPadOS 26 and iPhone 14 or newer are required. See [iPhone and iPad](#iphone-and-ipad) for what has been tested.

Without `-o`, the selected output appears next to the game file (`Tears of the Kingdom.app` on Mac or `Tears of the Kingdom.ipa` for iOS). Before full shader preparation was added, a local clean base-1.0.0 Mac build took about 6 minutes on an M4 Mac mini (this is not a timing estimate for the current build; hardware, disk and network conditions affect the time): about a minute each to rewrite the main code module and to decrypt the 17 GB of game data, and two to three minutes for macOS to check the finished app once. The current build then also prepares the startup shaders (about 3 minutes for 1.4.3 on an M4) and compiles them for your GPU (a few more minutes on an M4, but about 25 minutes on an 8 GB M1 MacBook Air, which runs out of memory and swaps during this step; without the Metal toolchain this step is skipped, with a message, while a game is running). A Mac build needs no .NET or CMake, and the finished game needs no Python: its shader translator is a native program that comes with this repository (`games/totk/prebuilt`). Every intermediate file is in a work folder next to the game file (`TOTK_build`, or `--work`); running the script again reuses what is already done.

The extracted code modules, rewritten modules, RomFS and shared fonts are checked against the selected version's `games/totk/assets/expected-v1.0.0.json`, `expected-v1.1.2.json`, `expected-v1.2.1.json` or `expected-v1.4.3.json`; the prebuilt shader translator has its own SHA-256 check. A mismatch stops the build, with one exception: a different genuine retail dump of the same version is accepted — its `main.npdm` is checked by Nintendo’s ACID signature (`npdm_signed()`) instead of the pinned hash, and its firmware’s shared fonts are checked for a valid BFTTF structure and bound by their actual SHA-256. Key values are never printed.

Signing and verifying a large updated app can add several minutes. Keep the build running while it continues to report progress.

**3. Play:** open the app from Finder. The build starts the launcher in `--check` mode, which checks that the game executable exists and allows macOS to perform its first-launch checks; it does not run a gameplay test. You can keep the app where it was built or move it to `/Applications`; the first start after a move compiles the shaders again in the background (macOS's Metal cache does not follow the app to its new place), so to keep it in `/Applications`, build it there with `-o`. Copying it to a different volume can use additional disk space and trigger another macOS check, during which no window may appear. The first game launch verifies the game data (about 20 seconds in local testing). Newly encountered shaders can cause stutters; cached shaders reduce this work on later visits.

### Build with a mod's code patches

```sh
python3.14 build_app.py ~/Games/totk.xci -k ~/keys/prod.keys --update ~/Games/1.4.3.nsp \
  --mod "/path/to/The Second Quest 1.4.3" --install-mod-romfs
```

`--mod` takes the mod folder as it comes, `exefs/` and `romfs/` together (either half alone works too). Why a build
flag at all: the app has no module loader - at start it maps the three code modules it was built from (main, sdk,
subsdk0), rewritten for Apple silicon and bound by SHA-256, and nothing in it reads a mod's `exefs/` the way Ryujinx or
a Switch does. So the code side goes in one step earlier: `--mod` merges the mod's main-module patches into the verified
retail module before it is rewritten.

The data side is a separate choice, because the version's mod folder is yours: `--install-mod-romfs` says the build may
replace it. With the flag, at the end of the build the folder
`~/Library/Application Support/MacNativeGames/TOTK/mods/<version>` is replaced by the mod's `romfs/` with a fresh
manifest written against the app just built (`make_mod_manifest.py`) - one command, an app that plays with the mod as it
stands. What the folder held is not deleted: it is moved next to it as `<version>.backup-<date>-<time>` (the game never
loads it), and the build says so when it starts and names the backup at the end, so add the flag only when that is what
you want; without it the build leaves the folder alone and prints the two commands that fill
it by hand. Several mods with code patches: merge them in the mod manager first (TKMM's output is one folder with one
`exefs/` and one `romfs/`), then build with `--mod <that folder> --install-mod-romfs`.
The patches are applied to the verified retail main of the version
being built - a `.pchtxt` as the game's own patch loader reads it, a `.ips` / `.ips32` with the emulator offset
convention - after checking that no edit lands on a site the app patches itself, that no two patches change the same
bytes and that every edit is inside main's own segments. The merged module is then rewritten for Apple silicon and the
app is bound to its SHA-256. `analysis/phase12-validation.json` (1.0.0) or `analysis/<version>-port/phase12-validation.json`
in `--work` records the mod folder, each patch file's SHA-256 and the addresses it changed, under `mod_exefs`. An extra
code module a mod ships (`subsdk9`, a hooking framework's) is not loaded and the build says so: such a mod keeps its
main patches and its RomFS, but not the code changes that live in that module. Step by step: [docs/mods.md](docs/mods.md).

To keep one desktop entry, link the packaged app with the optional installer:

```sh
python3.14 games/totk/tools/install_desktop_entry.py --app "/path/to/Tears of the Kingdom.app"
```

When replacing the older development launcher, the installer copies and verifies its saves into the standard user profile listed below and creates an upgrade backup. It preserves the original profile and archives the old launcher without adding another app entry. An existing, different standard profile is never overwritten.
